rationale: The parallel regnal notice gives Jotham the same accession age, sixteen-year reign, and maternal descent from Sadok, with a different spelling of his mother's name.

Jotham's towers and development outside Jerusalem continue the building activity described for his father, including wilderness towers and hill-country work; the sites and projects are not equated.
Father and son prosper through seeking or ordering their ways before the Lord, providing the stated religious explanation for their strength.
Both closing notices direct readers to a royal record for Jotham's other deeds, although they describe the record with different titles.
Both notices place Jotham's burial in David's city and name Ahaz as his successor.
Both give Ahaz's accession at twenty, his sixteen-year reign in Jerusalem, and his failure to follow David's righteous conduct.
Both connect Ahaz's conduct with Israel's kings; Kings specifies Jeroboam's way, while Chronicles adds the carved images.
Both accounts describe Ahaz making offspring pass through fire in imitation of the displaced nations; Chronicles speaks of children where Kings speaks of his son.
Ahaz adopts the precise kind of foreign worship forbidden here: imitating the nations and burning sons and daughters for their gods.
Both describe Ahaz sacrificing or burning incense at high places and under leafy trees; Chronicles has rooftops where Kings has hills.
Ahaz worships at the high and leafy-tree sites whose pagan altars Israel was commanded to destroy.
Kings identifies the Syrian and Israelite kings attacking Ahaz and reports Jerusalem's siege; Chronicles describes Judah's defeats and captives without making that siege a successful capture.
The explanation that Judah fell because it abandoned the Lord corresponds to the covenant warning of being delivered to slaughter before enemies; the law supplies no matching casualty total.

The capture of Judah's sons and daughters shares the covenant warning's loss of children, but the law speaks of another nation whereas the captors here are their Israelite brethren. No matching number or identical scenario is claimed.
Both passages distinguish God's anger against His people from the excessive violence of the attackers, who become objects of divine anger themselves.

Oded's objection to enslaving their Judean brethren accords with the law forbidding the reduction of an impoverished Israelite brother to household-slave service and harsh treatment; the legal setting is sale, not this battle.
The command to return captive brethren accords with the law's protection of Israelite kin and their return to family and ancestral possession, without identifying this release as a Jubilee.
The Ephraimite leaders' resistance to the returning army is the concrete response to Oded's warning against retaining the Judean captives; their personal identities are not inferred from other lists.
The rulers repeat the prophet's warning that keeping their brethren would add guilt and expose Israel itself to the Lord's wrath.
The warriors' surrender of captives and spoil implements the demanded release and the leaders' refusal to accept them as prisoners.

Both scenes connect Jericho with mercy toward stripped or injured people, the use of an animal for transport, and restorative care. The comparison does not identify the events or claim an explicit quotation.

The captives' care and return to their brethren enact the law's concern that an Israelite brother not be treated as a disposable slave and ultimately return to his kin; the account does not call this a Jubilee.
Kings supplies the message behind Ahaz's appeal: he calls himself Assyria's servant and asks deliverance from Syria and Israel.
Ahaz's request for a foreign king's rescue recalls the rebuke of Asa for trusting a foreign king instead of the Lord; the partners and circumstances differ.
Idumean attacks and deportations reverse the earlier scene in which Amaziah's Judah defeated Seir and killed its captives; no identity of the individual captives is implied.
The foreigners' conquest of Judean cities reverses Uzziah's earlier destruction of their walls and building of cities in their territory; the named towns are different.
The text explicitly makes Judah's military humiliation a consequence of Ahaz's departure from the Lord, corresponding to the covenant warning of defeat.

Kings records Ahaz's appeal and Assyria's attack on Damascus; Chronicles emphasizes that the Assyrian king instead became a source of injury to Ahaz. The two outcomes are not flattened into one report.
Both record Ahaz taking temple and royal treasure to pay the Assyrian king; Chronicles adds the rulers' resources and explicitly says the payment brought no help.
Affliction drives Ahaz farther from the Lord, whereas Manasseh's affliction leads him to humble prayer and restoration.
Kings describes Ahaz copying Damascus's altar and sacrificing upon it, supplying related concrete cultic actions beside Chronicles' account of his trust in Damascus's gods.
Ahaz's deliberate decision to seek and imitate foreign gods is exactly the inquiry into foreign worship prohibited in this law.
Both Ahaz and Amaziah adopt foreign gods after military encounters, and both accounts expose the failure of those gods to provide the imagined protection.
Kings likewise records Ahaz cutting temple fittings and altering temple access; Chronicles additionally states that he shut the doors and multiplied Jerusalem's altars.
Hezekiah's opening and repair of the temple doors directly reverses Ahaz's closure of them.
Ahaz constructs foreign high-place worship throughout Judah where the law requires pagan cult sites, altars, and images to be destroyed.
Both conclude Ahaz's deeds with a reference to royal records, using different descriptions of the record.
Both report Ahaz's death, burial in David's city, and Hezekiah's succession; Chronicles adds exclusion from the kings' tombs.
Both give Hezekiah's accession at twenty-five and reign of twenty-nine years, naming his mother as Zacharias or Zechariah's daughter with differing forms of her name.
Both judge Hezekiah's conduct by the same favorable comparison with David.
Opening and repairing the temple doors repairs the specific closure carried out by Ahaz.

Hezekiah summons the priests and Levites because their established ministry includes the temple courts, purification of holy things, and service alongside Aaron's sons; the east-side station is not supplied by the target.

The preceding account supplies Syrian deportation and deadly attacks as the background to Hezekiah's lament. The group taken to Samaria was subsequently returned in 28:11-15 and is not equated with all those still captive here.
Hezekiah's combination of military slaughter and captive sons and daughters corresponds to the covenant warnings of defeat, plunder, and loss of children.

The later Passover account again locates the singers' stations under the commands of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, explaining the continuing service of the named musical houses.

Finishing the temple cleansing on the sixteenth day of the first month helps explain why the following Passover is deferred while priestly purification and public assembly are still inadequate.
The cleansing finishes on the sixteenth day, after the ordinary Passover date of the fourteenth day of the first month; this supplies calendar context without redefining the lawful date.

The king and assembly laying hands on a sin offering resemble the law's communal procedure through the elders, while the target prescribes a calf and the restoration ceremony here uses male goats.

The use of a male goat's blood for the people and the explicit inclusion of all Israel resemble the law's communal atonement, without identifying this as the annual rite.
David's appointment of prophetic musicians with cymbals, nablai, and kinyrai supplies the earlier organization renewed by Hezekiah; Gad and Nathan are additional authorities named here.
The specified cymbals and stringed instruments continue David's instruction to organize Levitical psalm singers with those kinds of instruments.

The use of Asaph's words and his prophetic designation correspond to the earlier appointment of Asaph's house for inspired musical service.

Hezekiah's attribution of the people's readiness to God resembles David's joyful acknowledgment that the ability to offer willingly comes from God.

Inviting Israel as well as Judah reflects the command that the whole congregation of Israel observe the Passover.
The second-month celebration draws on the provision of a later Passover for those prevented by uncleanness or distant travel; the national decision here has its own stated circumstances.

The king and assembly approve the specific second-month proposal made in response to insufficient purification and attendance; the approval concerns that remedy, not a general change of calendar.
The proclamation throughout Israel implements the requirement that the whole congregation keep the Passover, answering the source's complaint about its inadequate observance.
Calling the people to Jerusalem rather than keeping Passover in their own cities follows the law's central-place requirement.
The call to return to the Lord with a promise of restored survivors follows the law's sequence of return, mercy, gathering, and restoration to the land.
The deportation of northern territories by the Assyrian king supplies concrete background for the appeal to survivors of Assyria; the target is not used to date every stage of Hezekiah's invitation.
The warning against repeating the fathers' apostasy invokes the same covenant pattern of disobedience bringing defeat and devastation.
The command not to stiffen their necks and to serve the Lord closely matches Moses' demand to end hardness of heart and serve God wholeheartedly.
The invitation to enter the sanctuary sanctified for ever recalls God's declaration that He had chosen and sanctified this house for His name for ever.
The promise that returning to God brings mercy and a return from captivity restates the covenant promise of compassion and regathering.
The invitation's promise of mercy for returning captives corresponds to Solomon's prayer for forgiveness when exiles turn back and pray toward the chosen city and house.
Mocking the royal messengers who call Israel back to God anticipates the later account's rejection and mockery of God's messengers; the messengers and occasions remain distinct.
Northerners coming to worship in Jerusalem continue the earlier pattern under Asa of people from Israel joining Judah when they recognized God's presence there.
The Lord's gift of one heart develops the preceding account's attribution of the people's sudden readiness for renewed worship to God.
The second-month assembly keeps Passover with unleavened bread as provided for those unable to observe it in the first month; the large national gathering is the narrative's circumstance.
Removing Jerusalem's false altars reverses Ahaz's installation of altars throughout the city.
The destruction of false-worship altars carries out the command to demolish pagan cult sites and their equipment.
The later reform under Josiah similarly removes false-worship objects and disposes of them in the Kidron area; the two cleansings are not equated.
The fourteenth day of the second month matches the alternative Passover date explicitly given in the law.
Both Passover accounts station priests and Levites in their assigned roles and have priests handle blood passed from the slaughtering service.
The priests' handling of sacrificial blood agrees with the law's assignment of altar blood service to Aaron's sons; the target concerns a burnt offering, not a complete Passover rule.
The later command for Levites to sacrifice the Passover for their brethren matches their practical assistance here to worshipers unable to prepare themselves.
The people eat despite remaining unpurified, whereas the law responds to uncleanness by postponing Passover. Hezekiah's prayer acknowledges the departure rather than declaring it ordinary compliance.
Hezekiah's plea for mercy on the people corresponds to the temple promise of divine pardon and healing in response to humble prayer and seeking God.
The prayer's appeal to hearts directed to seek God reflects the law's demand for wholehearted love and service; it does not erase the source's admitted deficiency in ritual purity.
The plea for those whose hearts seek God connects with the promise to hear, forgive, and heal those who humble themselves and seek His face.
The Lord's hearing and healing answer the earlier temple promise that He will hear repentant prayer and heal.

The sustained seven-day celebration corresponds to the law's feast following Passover with offerings each day; the second-month timing comes from the separate postponement provision.
The feast's salvation offerings and thanksgiving correspond to the law's sacrifice of praise and deliverance.

Hezekiah's encouragement of Levites showing understanding toward the Lord recalls the earlier description of trained temple singers singing with understanding; the offices are not restricted to those singers here.

At Josiah's later Passover, king and rulers likewise contribute large numbers of animals so the assembled people can celebrate; the totals are different.

The rejoicing participation of resident foreigners fits the Passover law's inclusion of the sojourner under the same observance as the native; the verse does not independently specify each participant's eligibility.
The law permits resident foreigners to keep Passover under its stated conditions and one common law, explaining their inclusion without assuming that the narrative reports every required preparation.

The divisions' duties of temple ministry, praise, and offerings reflect the detailed Levitical responsibilities recorded under David.

Hezekiah's provision for Sabbaths, new moons, and festivals renews the ordered calendar of offerings previously maintained under Solomon according to Moses.
Providing the Levites' portion so they can serve corresponds to the tithe given in return for their sanctuary ministry.

The livestock tithes correspond to the law declaring every tenth animal in the cattle and flock count holy to the Lord.

Azarias's report that the temple ministers have eaten from the firstfruits accords with the law assigning those gifts to the priestly household.
Preparing storage chambers for the consecrated contributions supplies facilities for the temple treasury function previously assigned to Levites.
Placing Chonenias and Semei over the stored gifts continues the established use of Levitical overseers for temple treasuries; the officials are not identified with the earlier men.
Kore's distribution of firstfruits and most holy things administers the offerings assigned by law to Aaron's priestly household, with distinct rules for the different classes of gifts.

The named agents carry out Kore's preceding distribution responsibility, showing how the gifts reach the priestly brethren by divisions, great and small; no external identity is assigned to the agents.
The enrollment of Levites from twenty years upward follows the service-age count recorded in David's final arrangements.
Enrollment of priests by ancestral houses continues the earlier division and written registration of Aaron's descendants for ministry.

Distribution to the enrolled Levites implements their allotted tithe support, including recipients living outside the immediate temple establishment.

Wholehearted seeking, obedience, and successful action here correspond to Kings' account of Hezekiah clinging to the Lord, keeping Moses' commandments, and having the Lord with him.
